questions.question: Your team has eight jobs of very different sizes and four teammates sharing one task list. Everyone takes the next job whenever they finish. Why does this usually finish faster than giving each person a fixed pile upfront?
options: Sharing a list means nobody sits idle while someone else is stuck with several long jobs.
A shared list lets the team skip the longest jobs entirely.
Fixed piles are faster because idle time helps computers cool down.
Taking the next job doubles the total amount of work to be done.
questions.explanation: Understanding how a shared task list balances uneven work prepares you for this lesson, which implements that pattern and shows what logging is needed to debug it.

questions.question: What workload does `make_tasks(4)` construct?
options: Four tasks, all lasting 0.4 seconds.
Eight tasks: four slow tasks at 0.4 s and four fast tasks at 0.1 s.
Eight tasks all lasting 0.1 seconds.
Sixteen tasks divided evenly among four fixed workers.
questions.explanation: The loop creates task ids 0–7; ids 0–3 are slow (0.4 s) and ids 4–7 are fast (0.1 s).

questions.question: Why is fixed assignment much slower than the swarm for this fixture?
options: Fixed assignment executes every task twice.
The queue adds a 0.4 s delay before any work begins.
Worker 0 receives all four slow tasks while other workers finish their fast tasks and idle.
The swarm skips the slow tasks rather than processing them.
questions.explanation: `make_tasks` assigns every slow task to worker 0. That worker serially spends about 1.6 s on them, whereas shared pulling lets all workers take slow tasks as capacity frees.

questions.question: What protects the swarm's per-worker counts when a task finishes?
options: The task's duration acts as a lock.
The main thread rewrites counts after all workers exit.
A global database transaction around every sleep.
A `threading.Lock` guards the increment, and `q.task_done()` marks queue completion.
questions.explanation: The worker performs `fake_work`, enters the lock to increment `counts[wid]`, then calls `task_done`. The queue itself hands out each task once.

questions.question: What string does `fake_work(Task(task_id=7, duration=0))` return?
options: `task-7-done`
`worker-7-complete`
`done:7:0`
An empty string because duration is zero
questions.explanation: `fake_work` sleeps for the supplied duration and returns `f"task-{task.task_id}-done"`, so the id appears in the result regardless of duration.

questions.question: What operational tradeoff does the demo state for the swarm pattern?
options: It has a central trace automatically, so no task ids are needed.
It balances variable work, but debugging needs per-task IDs and durable logs because there is no central trace.
It is useful only when every task has identical duration.
It guarantees exactly-once external side effects without a checkpoint.
questions.explanation: Shared pulling improves utilization when durations vary. The code also explicitly warns that decentralized execution needs task identifiers and durable logging for diagnosis.
